Once the various dhyānas have arisen,

afflictions will increase daily, giving rise to views and craving.

all such individuals are those who have given rise to faults because of dhyāna.

Although the nine dhyānas of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* are not the present subject matter, [they are mentioned for context].

moreover, within the nine dhyānas, there are those that include the dhyāna of active practice (saviṣaya-dhyāna). This is simply distinguished according to whether it pertains to one's own practice or to the transformation of others.

As for what are called the four dhyānas and eight samādhis:
Regarding the fourth point, where items are listed twice within the eightfold enumeration:
when the two realms of form and formlessness are contrasted,
the realm of form is termed *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) and the formless realm is termed *samādhi* (concentration).
If one considers the upper realms collectively in relation to the lower realm of desire,

then both of the upper two realms are termed "concentrated" (*samāhita*), while the lower realm of desire is termed "distracted" (*vikṣipta*). These constitute the nine [categories] such as the "innate nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth.
Both the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* clarify the nine [perfections] by means of the six pāramitās;
the names of these nine are identical in both,
as explained extensively therein.
This is a brief commentary and explanation of the *Dharmadhātu-krama*.

however, what is cited here for reference is a praise of them, not an exposition on their actual cultivation.
Next, within the section providing detailed explanations according to the chapters,
first is the clarification of the opening and closing [of the sections].
This begins by enumerating the ten gates of the present text.
Next, one should investigate their similarities and differences by means of five gates and fifteen gates.
Regarding the five gates:
This refers to the first five gates of the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) within the Hīnayāna.
Because both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna initially enter through them,
they are called "gates" (*mukha*).
The preceding section served as the means for entering into the principle by way of its counteractive measures;
therefore, the present text provides a comparative analysis.
As for the fifteen gates:
Since each of the five gates of cessation (*pañca-vipaśyanā-sthāna*) is further divided into three, there are fifteen;
thus, the various meditations on the great and small matters and principles fully encompass all teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
Now it is clarified that the cultivation and arousal [of the mind] pertain only to the dhyāna of phenomena (vastu-dhyāna),
while the principle belongs to the universal cultivation and the latter two objects;
therefore, the following text says:
If there were only five gates, some things would not be included;
if one were to adopt fifteen meanings, they would become confused with the underlying principle.
Now, in order to expand upon what was concise, the five are opened into ten.
Since the underlying principle is removed while the phenomena remain, fifteen items have been condensed into ten.
Fearing that people might not understand the number of categories,
I have thus indicated the intent behind both opening and closing, as well as what is excluded and what is retained.
Therefore, we now employ ten categories to respond to and analyze the questions and answers regarding the extensive and concise [teachings].
Thus it is said: "The ten gates and the five gates, etc.
What are their similarities and differences?
In the response, there is first a general explanation,
followed by a detailed one.
Within the detailed explanation, five gates are opened to form ten gates.
However, for those who are deficient in matters among these five,
the practice is further opened up;
if there are no matters that require such opening, then it remains as is.
Thus, one preserves the practice and maintains the fundamental;
this is why counting the breaths and the meditation on impurity are opened up as belonging to the realm of phenomena (*vastu*).
One follows these openings and closings to grasp [the truth].
Therefore, these two gates, together with the original one, each consist of three [sections].
Regarding mindfulness of the Buddha through the causal conditions of a compassionate mind,
these three have no further points to be expanded upon.

Regarding the *Abhidharma* explanation of "the skillful means of the realms" (*dhātu-upāya*),
it is as cited in the seventh section on the Aids to Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
Supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) were not previously included among the five gates;
however, since they arise from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and exist within all nine gates, it is necessary to clarify them here.
Thus, the first two [gates] are opened but not closed;
the next three are closed but not opened;
and the single gate of supernormal powers is neither opened nor closed.
Taken collectively, these five gates are both opened and closed.
Next, to clarify how the fifteen are condensed into ten:
the first six gates are opened and not condensed.
Next, there are nine gates which are condensed into three.
Regarding the three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), only that which takes sentient beings as its object is adopted;
the other two are omitted.
This is because the objectless [contemplation] based on dharmas belongs to the principle.
If one were to open it up so that it belongs to the realm of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas,
then one would open up the dharma-based [contemplation] to belong to the two vehicles.
The "objectless" (anālambana) [contemplation] belongs to Bodhisattvas.
The text does not distinguish them individually but refers generally to both objects;
for the objects of the two vehicles are exclusively those of the "dharma-object" (dharmālambana).
The Bodhisattva, however, penetrates both the conditioned and the unconditioned;
therefore, they are not distinguished or treated separately. Question:

If it is without conditions (*anālambana*), it should pertain to the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Stage (*pariniṣpanna-bodhisattva*). Why, then, is it said to be within the sphere of the Bodhisattva? Answer:
First, the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*) also belongs to the objectless (*wuyuan*).
Second, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is also provisionally situated within the realm of the Bodhisattvas and explained thereafter.
Furthermore, the stages prior to the [first] stage of the Distinct Teaching belong to the object of sentient beings (*zhongsheng yuan*) and the object of phenomena (*fayuan*).
The same applies up through the seventh bhūmi.
For the Tripiṭaka Bodhisattvas, throughout the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, their compassion is entirely that directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambanā maitrī*).
Here, we are considering the point at which the Bodhisattva first becomes distinct from the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and from ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, the "conditioned by objects" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the "unconditioned" (*anālambana*) are collectively indicated as being explained within those two types of objects.
Next, regarding the gate of the "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*), it exists only in the three time periods;
because the two other periods and a single moment are subtle, they are subsumed under principle.
What is called "retribution" refers to the two time periods [past and future].
A single thought-moment is a *kṣaṇa*.
This is fully as cited previously in the seventh and eighth fascicles.
Although these two causes and conditions are not the principle itself, their subtle meaning accords with the principle;
therefore, they also belong to the category of the principle.

Within the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma-body and Reward-body belong to the realm of principle (*li*);
since this meaning is easy to understand, it is not treated separately.

since the supernormal powers (abhijñā) depend upon the dhyāna of the phenomenal realm (vastu-dhyāna),
they also belong to the phenomenal realm.
Regarding the phrase "although they may be expanded or condensed":
if condensed into five, they are sufficient for the purpose of counteracting hindrances;
thus, they can generally serve as skillful means for entering the Path.
Expanding [the categories], there are fifteen for the purpose of subsuming the principles and phenomena of the contemplative methods of the Great and Small Vehicles;
condensing them, there are ten gates for the purpose of judging the cultivation of the Dharma.

First, I shall briefly refute these two theories.
Both theories judge that *śamatha* (calm abiding) involving objects is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
whereas the wisdom of the truths that empties the mind is alone termed without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Now, a brief summary is provided below.
Since this does not constitute a complete negation, it is said to be "slightly different.
Here, it is clarified that the dhyāna of phenomena (vastu-dhyāna) is with outflows (sāsrava).
As stated in the two treatises,
the wisdom that does not take the truths as its object differs from the views of those two schools;
hence it is said that a melon can act as a condition for illness.
The same applies to the tainted (sāsrava): they take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object, just as the fundamental dhyānas do;
for while the fundamental [dhyānas] are themselves tainted, they do not [themselves] become untainted.
However, because one cultivates only the fundamental [meditation], it is said that "exclusive cultivation" belongs to the outflowing (sāsrava) category;
this applies even to the four [practices] such as self-cultivation and transforming others.
Both are termed "with outflows" (sāsrava),
as detailed below in the text.
Because they are not exclusively with outflows, it is said that they are "minor" and should be analyzed accordingly.
The "forty-eight years" refers to the citation of evidence for the existence of outflows (āsrava);
the four categories, such as one's own practice, each consist of twelve gates.
Therefore, all forty-eight [years] are with outflows (*sāsrava*).
In that second sutra, the old physician says to the new physician:
"If you can now follow me as my servant for forty-eight years..."
Only after that shall I instruct you in the medical arts.
Regarding these forty-eight [points], there have been many interpretations in antiquity.
The Master said:
Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the Buddha] was still a disciple of non-Buddhist paths;
hence it is said that he spent forty-eight years [in this state]. Kaishan said:
Each of the eight dhyānas has six aspects;
hence, it is said there are forty-eight. Zhan’an said:
Each of the four views has three provisional [categories], and each provisional category has four propositions.
Thus, the three provisional categories together comprise forty-eight.
If, according to the Āgamas, a non-Buddhist practitioner must first undergo forty-eight years [of training], [this corresponds to these forty-eight categories].
Only after providing him with attendants and messengers does one then administer the medicine;
the text here precisely corresponds to the method of the old physician.
The new physician temporarily adopts the same method as the old physician.
This is called "following the messenger. If that is so,
then the Āgama sūtras and the two sets of forty-eight [verses] cited here should both accord with this meaning.
Therefore, the current text states:
"The four practices, such as self-practice, combined amount to forty-eight.
As for the twelve gates:"
The four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the four immeasurable minds. Furthermore,
the first fascicle of the *Benye yingluo jing* (Sutra on the Ornament of Fundamental Karma), in its explanation of the entry into the illusion-like samādhi within the tenth stage,
also clarifies the twelve gates of dhyāna.

Ānanda asked the Buddha,

"For what reason did the five hundred bhikṣus receive no benefit at all from the Dharma being preached to them by those who followed the turning of the Wheel of Dharma?
The Buddha said:
In the past, under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, this bhikṣu went forth as a monk with the name Ajita Nanda.
He was clever and possessed great wisdom, yet he was arrogant and heedless.
Failing to cultivate the foundations of mindfulness,
at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the Dark Hell.
Having emerged from that hell, they become nāgas for five hundred lifetimes.
For five hundred lifetimes he was a monkey;
by the power of his previous observance of the precepts, he was again born in the heavens.
When his celestial lifespan was exhausted, he came to be born among humans.
Due to the power of his previous recitation of the Tripiṭaka, he has now encountered a Buddha;
yet, because of his negligence, he does not yet realize it.
The Buddha therefore taught him the method of the contemplation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā).
First, begin from the first joint of the big toe of the foot.
In this manner, practice according to the sequence of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).

it should not be called "contemplation with outflows" (*sāsrava-dhyāna*).

therefore, it is said that when the Buddha taught this Dharma and the followers of the Two Vehicles practice it,

how then can it be said that it is not something known by those of the Two Vehicles?

therefore, they are rebuked as being ignorant.

since the practices of the Two Vehicles are also called "noble practices" (ārya-caryā),
all types of mundane dhyāna likewise belong to Bodhisattvas.

As for the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* passages cited regarding the nine perceptions (navasaṃjñā) and so forth:
The nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) are able to open the way to all [meditations on] impurity;
therefore, the great and small impurities, the great and small liberations (*vimokṣa*), as well as the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*),
all take the nine perceptions as their initial gateway.

Because impurity is established, the foundation of mindfulness of the body is established. Because the foundation of mindfulness of the body is established, the other three foundations of mindfulness are established.
Because the four foundations of mindfulness are established, all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are simultaneously established.
Therefore, it should not be exclusively impure (*sāsrava*).
The analogy of the two stones illustrates that various mundane dhyānas (*vastu-dhyāna*) can give rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
It is like the southern stone, which is cold by nature.
The northern stone is hot in nature.

why should it be restricted solely to the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*) and so forth?

In order to attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Answer:
If it were definitive, there would only be six stages (*bhūmi*).

if one were to include the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), it should be called nine stages,
by adding the three formless attainments (ārūpya) to the aforementioned six stages.

because they follow the perspective of individuals, both the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), the *anāgamya*, and the *antara* are all present.

according to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is said that among these ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*), the first three sever the views (*dṛṣṭi*), the [next] four sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the final three pertain to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This shall first be compared with the *Gradual Gate of Dhyāna* (*Cidi Chanmen*).
Since each possesses both sharp and dull faculties, their respective sequences differ.
Within that *Dhyāna Gate*, the chapters are arranged in a specific order.
In the sixth chapter, which elucidates skillful means (*upāya*), it says:
"There are two kinds of skillful means, namely the external and the internal.
The external refers to the twenty-five dharmas."
Internally, there are five distinct gates:
first, cessation;
second, examining the roots and natures of good and evil.
Third, settling the mind;
fourth, treating illness;
fifth, demonic activities.
The gate of cessation (*śamatha*) further consists of three parts:
first, binding the object of focus;
second, restraining the mind.
The third is the True Body.
Following the Cessation of the True Body,
the five wheels are clearly manifested.
It is only after the five wheels of dhyāna have been practiced that one’s capacity for good or evil roots is verified;
therefore, it is said that in the Chan school, one first gives rise to [the mind] and later verifies its goodness or evil.
Furthermore, once the mind has been aroused in the Chan school...
Furthermore, each of these is verified by means of the gates of good and evil;
good and evil are karma,
along with illnesses, demonic activities, and so forth.
Furthermore, following the Five Wheels of Dhyāna,
this text first obstructs the realms of afflictions, karma, and māras,
and only thereafter does dhyāna arise.
Therefore, one should know that the sharp and the dull are not the same.
This is based merely on the characteristics of their arising as presented in the preceding and following passages;
thus, the two instances concerning the sharp and the dull differ in their underlying intent.
If, in the present text, one first contemplates the aggregates and sense bases,
one will immediately give rise to the various dhyānas and further achieve the benefits of dhyāna.
